commenti.body:
I'm with your take on this pretty much 100 percent. I think it's a movie that asks us to do some of the work as well. It seems the negative responses I've seen are from viewers who want the same Holocaust movie with the same conventions and the same tropes (e.g. the bit of hope in the midst of hopelessness, the psychopathic or sinister nazi big boss with his senseless brutalities) but this movie definitely doesn't provide any of that. By not showing us what we've seen in other movies and read in books, and not showing us what's on the other side of the wall, even though we know all too well what's there, it forces us to think about it again, The Holocaust. 

I think this movie leans into the reality that, whether the real Hoss was a sociopath or not, many career nazis who did unspeakable things weren't sociopaths. They just chose not to think about it. They just lived their lives and did their jobs with all the concern of a foreman making sure that things were running smoothly on the factory  floor, even though their jobs, in this case, involved the mass extermination of countless human beings. It's unthinkable. And they didn't spend much time thinking of it. 

When the mother comes and flees, we are reminded that no matter how much the mundane rhythm of their lives has lulled these people into an acceptance of a nightmare, it is an absolute nightmare all around them. They refuse to see it. They refuse to think it. But fresh eyes and ears and noses and hearts and brains and souls cannot miss it!

It's interesting to me that, even though they had 2 childred in real life, the script expands it to 5 kids. I have a theory on this that jibes with the fresh hearts thing. The baby is always crying, and a lot of the soundscaping made it confusing if its the Hoss' baby or a baby in the camp or what. But the baby is often in a state of distress. The younger boy and girl also have some disturbances. 

The young girl is a sleepwalker and insomniac, and the episodes of her sleeplessness and her father reading the fairytale to her, often lead into the real life girl who hides the apples at the work sites. (Btw, it's very interesting that those scenes are the only ones shown in negative, since her character is the only one not accepting what's happening; she's at odds or in relief to the reality all around her.) But I think the Hoss' daughter has a subconscious impulse to help as well. 

The younger boy is also shown wary and worried at times, which is more emotion than his parents or older siblings ever show. When he listens by the window, he seems vaguely disturbed by what is going to happen to the prisoner. His older brother is more callous, looking at dental filings before bed and locking his little brother in the greenhouse against his will, symbolically like it's an oven. 

There's the banality of evil theme, of course, but it seems that the film is showing that there's a boiling the frog aspect to it, that anyone with their heart and mind and senses still intact wouldn't be able to stand it for a second, but that these people have slowly become inured to absolute evil.

I think they've trained themselves not to think about it so much that when Hoss goes to the doctor for an abdominal exam and we see him wretching on the steps it's his body revolting, even though he's trained his mind not to, his body cannot stand the lie and horror of it all.
